patient.chief_complaint: Found unresponsive in bed by family, brief shaking witnessed earlier, persistent confusion now 55 minutes
patient.history_present_illness: A 77-year-old White female retired librarian was brought to the emergency department by her son after she was found increasingly difficult to rouse this morning. Her son reports she lives alone and had called him last night complaining of a headache and feeling 'fuzzy-headed.' When he arrived this morning, she was in bed, and he witnessed what he described as generalized stiffening and rhythmic jerking of her arms and legs lasting approximately 2 minutes. After the shaking stopped, she was still not back to normal. He called 911. On EMS assessment, 30 minutes after the observed seizure, she was awake but staring blankly, answering only 'yes' or 'no,' with significant word-finding difficulty. She has a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and moderate Alzheimer's dementia. She lives alone with daily check-ins from her son. Her baseline per son is that she is oriented to her name and sometimes the year, speaks in short sentences, needs help with medications, but is independent with basic ADLs. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation, donepezil, and lisinopril. Her son reports her INR was therapeutic at her last check 3 weeks ago (2.4). However, she has been taking several doses of over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain for the past 10 days. She has no prior history of seizures. No recent falls per son. Temperature at scene 38.0°C per EMS. Urine was foul-smelling per son who changed her pad this morning. Son suspects urinary tract infection.

interactions: Warfarin + ibuprofen (NSAID): MAJOR interaction — NSAIDs potentiate warfarin anticoagulant effect via displacement of warfarin from plasma protein binding sites (raising free warfarin concentration) and inhibition of COX-1 platelet function; the combination increases hemorrhagic risk.

Concurrent NSAID use in patients on warfarin is associated with significantly increased risk of supratherapeutic INR and bleeding complications; the magnitude of INR elevation is variable and unpredictable.
NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin-mediated renal afferent arteriolar vasodilation, which may result in acute kidney injury, particularly in at-risk patients.
contraindications: NSAIDs with warfarin: contraindicated without close INR monitoring — risk of life-threatening hemorrhage
warnings: NSAIDs should be avoided in patients on warfarin; if analgesia is required, acetaminophen is preferred at standard doses.
Monitor INR closely when concurrent interacting medications are introduced or discontinued.
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) and vitamin K are established reversal agents for warfarin-associated coagulopathy requiring urgent reversal.

results.title: Restarting anticoagulation after subdural hematoma: systematic review
results.key_finding: Risk-benefit for anticoagulation restart after SDH: CHADS2-VASc score vs HAS-BLED score must be balanced. CAA pattern on MRI significantly increases hemorrhagic recurrence risk. Consider alternative direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban) which have lower intracranial hemorrhage risk than warfarin. Restart generally after 4-8 weeks for low-moderate bleeding risk; individual decision for high-risk (CAA, elderly).

output.summary: Anticoagulation restart after subdural hematoma requires balancing thromboembolic risk (estimated by CHADS2-VASc score) against hemorrhagic recurrence risk (estimated by HAS-BLED score and imaging findings). Cerebral amyloid angiopathy on MRI (lobar microhemorrhages by Boston criteria) is associated with higher risk of recurrent intracranial hemorrhage, which is relevant when weighing anticoagulation decisions. Direct oral anticoagulants (e.g., apixaban) have demonstrated lower rates of intracranial hemorrhage compared to warfarin in randomized trials in atrial fibrillation. Timing of anticoagulation restart after SDH is variable; most observational data suggest 4-8 weeks in appropriate patients. Concurrent NSAID use with anticoagulants is associated with markedly increased hemorrhagic risk and requires close monitoring.

red_herrings.data_point: Urinalysis: WBC >50 cells/hpf, nitrites positive, many gram-negative rods; temperature 38.2°C; WBC 14.6
red_herrings.intended_effect: Strongly suggests UTI-related sepsis encephalopathy as the primary cause of confusion and seizure — prompting empiric antibiotics and sepsis workup without urgent CT head, potentially delaying life-saving SDH diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: UTI is a real secondary precipitant that lowered seizure threshold but cannot alone cause focal NCSE with right hemisphere lateralization; the critical INR 4.8, focal neurological signs (left facial droop, right Babinski), and CT confirming 12 mm SDH establish the structural diagnosis; CT head must precede any LP in an anticoagulated patient with focal signs

red_herrings.data_point: Sodium 130 mEq/L (moderate hyponatremia) with AKI (Creatinine 1.4) and metabolic acidosis (CO2 20)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests metabolic encephalopathy from hyponatremia as the cause of seizure, prompting sodium correction as primary treatment and potentially overlooking the structural SDH
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia 130 mEq/L lowers seizure threshold and contributes to the clinical picture, but focal NCSE from right temporal-parietal region cannot be explained by hyponatremia alone (which causes generalized not focal seizures); the SDH is the primary structural driver; hyponatremia results from ibuprofen-induced water retention combined with UTI-related SIADH
